questions.problem:
What is the common difference for the following arithmetic sequence?

$$
-5,\,-12,\,-19,\,-26,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The common difference $d$ of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common difference for our sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =-12-(-5) \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the three sequences below are arithmetic sequences?

I. $-2,\,-4,\,-6,\,-8,...$

II. $-2,\,-9,\,-16,\,-23,...$

III. $-2,\,4,\,10,\,16,...$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine whether each sequence is an arithmetic sequence, we need to look at the jumps between terms in the sequence. If the jumps are the same, then they indeed represent a common difference of an arithmetic sequence. 

- In sequence I, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence I is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14203588/assets/c599604e6630b0dbf74d646f93b6330b5d310f35bfbce7b008f16d1686534c77.png)

- In sequence II, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence II is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-7.$

- In sequence III, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence III is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14203588/assets/9aa43107c2b5c975450590f4bc126273b45ddc72f1acfd3d35eadff0313ded1b.png)

In conclusion, sequences I, II, and III are arithmetic sequences.

canonical_examples.problem:
What is the common difference of the following arithmetic sequence?

$$
7,\: 2,\: -3,\: -8,\: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The common difference $d$ of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common difference for our sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =2-7 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following sequence:

$$
1,\quad 3,\quad 5,\quad 7,\quad 9,\quad \ldots
$$

Notice that the difference (or "jump") between two consecutive numbers is always the same. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14203588/assets/5a4433d95492b9895793bc497fce887e3a39986a4f0c686ebe8a5d9b54d4f3dc.png)

A sequence where the jump never changes is called an **arithmetic sequence.** 

We call this jump the **common difference**, and represent it using the letter $d.$ In this particular case, the common difference is $d=2.$
